notes.meaning: Job lived in the land of Uz, outside Israel, before the law of Moses was given. He was an upright man of complete integrity who loved God and deliberately stayed away from evil. Being blameless did not mean he was entirely sinless, but that he lived an honest life free from hypocrisy.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Job is presented as a non-Israelite living in a foreign land such as Edom, showing that wisdom literature often looked beyond Israel's borders.

notes.meaning: Job was blessed with ten children and huge herds of sheep, camels, oxen, and donkeys. In the ancient world, these large numbers pictured full divine favor and great honor. He also had a large household of servants and was respected as the greatest man in the entire region.

Job's grown sons took turns hosting family feasts in their homes, making sure to invite their three sisters to eat and drink with them. These regular meals showed a close, peaceful family that enjoyed celebrating together in harmony.

Whenever a cycle of feasting ended, Job gathered his children to purify themselves and offered burnt sacrifices for each one early in the morning. A burnt offering was a sacrifice given to seek God's forgiveness and favor. As the priest of his home, Job cared deeply about his children's hearts and wanted to cover any careless or sinful thoughts they might have had toward God.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The traditional Latin Vulgate translates the phrase as 'blessed God' because the Hebrew text uses the word for blessing as a polite substitute to avoid writing a curse against God.

notes.meaning: The angels, called the sons of God, gathered before the Lord in heaven to give an account of their duties, and Satan arrived among them. Even though Satan is God's great enemy, he remains a created being who must answer to the Almighty and can do nothing without God's permission.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The Hebrew title here is 'the accuser,' portraying this figure as a prosecuting attorney within God's heavenly court rather than the fully developed figure of the devil seen in later texts.

notes.meaning: The Lord asked Satan where he had been, and Satan replied that he had been roaming back and forth across the earth. God asked this question to demand a formal report, not because he was missing any knowledge. Satan's answer reveals that he actively patrols the world, looking for opportunities to cause harm.

The Lord pointed out Job to Satan, praising him as an upright servant with unmatched integrity who turned away from evil. God openly celebrated Job's true godliness before the adversary. This shows that Job's coming trials were not caused by personal sin or divine anger, but began with God's delight in his character.
Satan scoffed at God's praise, asking if Job served the Lord for nothing. He claimed that Job's godliness was purely selfish and driven by personal gain rather than real love for God.

Satan pointed out that God had placed a protective wall around Job, his family, and everything he owned. Because God blessed his work, his herds covered the land. The accuser claimed that anyone would appear faithful if they enjoyed such complete safety and endless prosperity.

Satan dared God to take away all of Job's wealth, insisting that Job would immediately curse God to his face. The devil was certain that without his riches, Job's devotion would turn into open rebellion.

The Lord placed all of Job's possessions into Satan's power, but strictly forbade him to harm Job's own body. God set the exact limits for this test to prove that Job's faith was real. Satan then left God's presence to begin his attacks.

The disaster began while Job's children were enjoying a meal and drinking wine in their oldest brother's home. Satan timed the strikes for a day of joyful celebration to make the sudden shock even more painful.

A messenger rushed to Job with news that desert raiders had attacked while the oxen were plowing and the donkeys grazed nearby. The Sabeans carried off the livestock and killed the servants with swords, leaving only one man alive to bring the report.

Before the first runner finished, a second messenger reported that fire from heaven had burned up the sheep and the shepherds. This destructive lightning made it look like God himself was attacking Job from the sky, leaving just one servant to share the terrible news.

While that servant was still speaking, a third arrived to report that three bands of Chaldean raiders had seized all three thousand camels. They slaughtered the workers, and only a single survivor managed to escape.

A fourth messenger came immediately with the most heartbreaking report of all. A violent desert wind struck the four corners of the house where Job's sons and daughters were feasting, collapsing the building and killing them all.

Job stood up, tore his robe, and shaved his head, following ancient customs that showed deep sorrow and shock. Yet instead of cursing God, he fell to the ground in worship. His heart was broken with grief, but he still chose to bow before his Creator.

Job recognized that he had entered the world with nothing, and he would leave it with nothing. He confessed that the Lord gave every blessing and that the Lord had the full right to remove them. Instead of turning bitter as Satan predicted, Job blessed God's holy name.

differ.view: God is completely sovereign over every loss, and Satan's actions are ultimately guided by God's purpose, so Job spoke truth when he said God took his blessings away.
God permits suffering and works through it, but Satan was the true instigator of these tragedies, so God is not the direct author of evil or pain.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Ancient Greek and Latin manuscripts add the words, 'as it pleased the Lord, so is it done,' emphasizing humble submission to divine providence.

notes.meaning: In all of these crushing tragedies, Job did not sin or accuse God of doing anything wrong. He refused to charge God with acting unfairly, proving that his faith was genuine and proving Satan's slander wrong.
